/blog/small-office-network-setup-guide.title: Small Office Network Setup: A Practical Guide for Business Owners
/blog/small-office-network-setup-guide.excerpt: A plain-language guide to setting up a small office network: capacity planning, wired backbones, VLANs, Wi-Fi coverage, security basics and maintenance.
/blog/small-office-network-setup-guide.html:
Most small office networks are not designed — they accumulate. A router here, an extension there, a mesh unit someone bought on sale. This guide explains what a properly planned small office network looks like, in plain language.

Start with capacity, not hardware

Before buying anything, count what the network must carry. Every laptop, phone, printer, IP camera, smart TV and doorbell counts — often 2–3 devices per person. Then estimate peak concurrent use and plan for two to three years of growth.

Wire what matters

Wi-Fi is for mobility. Fixed devices — desktops, printers, access points, cameras — should be wired. Wired connections are faster, more stable and far easier to diagnose.

  • Cat6 cabling run to every desk and key location, terminated at a patch panel
  • A managed switch (not a consumer 8-port box hidden behind a cupboard)
  • Everything labelled — future-you will be grateful

Segment the network

This is the step most small offices skip, and it is the one that matters most. Using VLANs, split the network into at least three segments: staff, guest and devices (cameras, IoT, printers). Firewall rules between them mean a guest device can never reach your accounting folder, and a compromised IP camera cannot be a stepping stone to your file server.

Wi-Fi that actually covers

Wi-Fi problems are usually placement problems. Enterprise-grade access points placed where people actually work — not where the internet line enters the building — beat any consumer router.

Security basics that are non-negotiable

  • Change every default password — router, switch, cameras, DVR
  • Enable the firewall and set a default-deny posture for inbound traffic
  • Use a VPN for remote access. Never expose Remote Desktop directly to the internet
  • Keep firmware updated — set a quarterly reminder if nothing else exists

Plan for maintenance on day one

A network is not a purchase; it is a system that needs attention. Core equipment should sit on a UPS, a basic monitoring setup should alert you before users do, and a documented diagram should exist so any technician can understand the setup in ten minutes.

Key takeaways
  • Size for growth, not for today’s headcount
  • Wire fixed devices; use Wi-Fi for mobility
  • Segment staff, guest and device traffic with VLANs
  • Change default passwords and use VPN for remote access
  • Document and maintain from day one

If reading this made you think of three things your current setup does wrong — that is a useful list to bring to a consultation. Talk to us and we will assess your network honestly.

/blog/3-2-1-backup-rule-explained.title: The 3-2-1 Backup Rule, Explained for Businesses
/blog/3-2-1-backup-rule-explained.excerpt: What the 3-2-1 backup rule means, why single-copy backups fail, and how to build a backup strategy your business can actually restore from.
/blog/3-2-1-backup-rule-explained.html:
Every business knows it should back up. Fewer businesses can actually restore — which is the only thing a backup is for. The 3-2-1 rule is the simplest framework that separates the two.

What 3-2-1 means

3 copies of your data — the original plus two backups. 2 different types of storage media. 1 copy kept offsite, or offline. Each number exists because a specific, common failure kills backups that ignore it.

Why single-copy backups fail

The most common "backup" — a copy on an external drive sitting next to the computer — fails in three ways at once. Ransomware encrypts every attached drive it can reach, including your backup. Theft or fire takes the original and the copy together. And accidental deletion, if your backup software merely syncs, deletes the backup copy too.

Choosing the second medium

Practical combinations for a small business: internal storage plus a NAS; internal storage plus cloud backup; or a NAS plus rotated external drives. What matters is that the two copies do not share a single point of failure.

The "1" that saves you

The offsite or offline copy is what stands between a ransomware event and a business-ending one. Cloud backup satisfies offsite. An external drive that is disconnected after each backup run satisfies offline. Increasingly, backup systems also offer immutable or versioned storage, where old copies cannot be altered or deleted for a set period.

Test the restore, not the backup

A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis, not a plan. Run a restore drill at least quarterly: recover a file, a folder and — at least once — a whole system. Note how long it takes. That number is your realistic downtime during an incident.

Getting started this week

  1. List the data your business cannot operate without
  2. Check where its existing copies live — all of them
  3. Close the gaps against 3-2-1: a second medium, an offsite or offline copy
  4. Confirm backups are versioned, not just synced
  5. Book a quarterly restore test on the calendar
Key takeaways
  • 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite or offline
  • Sync-only "backups" propagate deletions and ransomware
  • Immutable or versioned storage defeats backup encryption
  • Untested backups are a hypothesis — run restore drills

If you are unsure how your current setup scores against 3-2-1, ask us for a backup and recovery review — it is one of the highest-value assessments a business can get.

/blog/website-vs-web-app-vs-mobile-app.title: Website, Web App or Mobile App: Choosing the Right Build
/blog/website-vs-web-app-vs-mobile-app.excerpt: A practical decision framework for choosing between a website, a custom web application and a mobile app — cost, maintenance and use cases explained.
/blog/website-vs-web-app-vs-mobile-app.html:
"We need an app" is a sentence that hides three very different projects with very different costs. This guide gives you the decision framework we use in consultations.

Three different tools

A website is how the world finds and evaluates you — brochure, catalogue, credibility. A web application is a tool a defined team uses to run operations: a CRM, inventory system, booking engine or internal dashboard. A mobile app is software that lives in a specific person’s pocket, using device capabilities — camera, GPS, notifications — to deliver something at the moment it is needed.

The decision factors

  • Who uses it, and how often? The open public, occasionally → website. A defined team, daily → web app. Customers or field staff, on the move → mobile app.
  • Does it need device hardware? Camera scanning, GPS tracking, push notifications, offline capture — these push you toward mobile.
  • What is the total cost of ownership? Every build is a running system: hosting, updates, security patches, support. Budget for the next five years, not the launch.

A simple decision path

If your audience needs to find you, start with a website. If a team uses a system daily to run the business, build a web application. If customers need you in their pocket with device features, build a mobile app.

Where hybrid fits

Cross-platform frameworks let one codebase ship to both Android and iOS — usually the sensible choice when the app does not depend on platform-specific performance. Progressive Web Apps can give app-like behavior from a website.

Key takeaways
  • Website = being found; web app = running operations; mobile app = being in the pocket
  • Budget for total ownership, not just the launch
  • Cross-platform first, native when the case demands it
  • Start with the cheapest version that proves the idea

If you are weighing these options, talk to us — we will tell you honestly when a simpler build is the smarter one.

/privacy.title: Privacy Policy
/privacy.excerpt: How SOWRIX Technologies collects, uses and protects personal information submitted through this website, including contact data, job applications and resume storage.
/privacy.html:
1. What we collect

When you submit our contact form, we collect the details you provide: your name, company, contact information, location, service interest, budget range and project description. When you apply for a job, we collect your name, contact information, location, experience, skills, LinkedIn/portfolio links, cover letter and resume.

2. How we use it

Contact form data is used solely to respond to your enquiry, prepare proposals and provide services you request. Job application data is used only for recruitment evaluation. We do not sell your data. We do not add you to marketing lists without consent.

3. Storage and security

Enquiry and application data is stored on secured systems with access limited to the team handling your request. Resume access is restricted to authorized recruitment staff. Automated malware scanning is not enabled in this release. We apply reasonable technical and organizational measures appropriate to the sensitivity of the data.

4. Retention

We retain enquiry data only as long as needed to handle your request and any follow-on engagement. Job applications are retained for up to 12 months after the role is closed, unless you request earlier deletion.

5. Your rights

You may request access to, correction of, or deletion of your personal data by contacting us at the email below.

6. Third parties

We do not share your data with third parties except where required to deliver a service you requested (e.g. authorized e-waste recyclers handling your decommissioned assets), or where legally required.

7. Cookies & analytics

This website is built to function without tracking cookies. If analytics is enabled, it is configured with privacy-respecting settings. See our Cookie Policy for details.
